Short Rest

During short rest scenes, for every 2 PCs in the party one of them can perform an activity.

You should rotate among yourselves and avoid consecutive repeats.

Long Rest

We call the times when the heroes retire for the day at a safe location (such as a settlement or at camp) long rests. In these locations the heroes are able to restock their supplies, unwind and fully prepare for their next day.

During long rest scenes, each PC fully recovers their hit points, mind points, inventory points and clears all their tension points.

We define a Journey in the system as the activity performed when the party travels from their current location to a distant one over the course of one day or more.

When there is risk involved, we call that a journey and make use of the rules in this section. Each journey will begin with a travel check.

Travel Check

Once the heroes have decided on a destination and have confirmed they are setting out, the party will make a travel check. A player can volunteer one of their heroes to make the check using the dice listed below.

Location

Danger Level

Travel Check

Settlements

Low

D4

Road

Moderate

D6

Wilderness

High

D8

Remote Locale

Severe

D10

Hazardous Locale

Extreme

D12

  • On a result of 6 or higher, the party encounters a danger.

  • On a result of 1, the party makes a discovery.

After the check and its resulting event is resolved, the party will enter a long rest scene at their Camp. Here the heroes can unwind, work on their downtime projects and deepen their relationships.

Most journeys can be resolved with a single travel check. Refrain from making more than that unless it's a very long journey lest you bog down your session.

Dangers

Hazard

The party can encounter a natural hazard, which will be taxing to traverse.

Ambush

The party can be beset upon by hostile creatures.

Loss

The party loses an important item or a piece of equipment. Let the players volunteer it.

Villain

The party can encounter a villain or one of their associates.

Discoveries

One of the most positive outcomes of a travel check is that of a discovery, which can be one of the following.

Location

An entrance to an abandoned keep. A waterfall with a hidden entrance behind it. All of these are locations where exciting developments can occur and where danger lurks. A chance for the heroes to test themselves and learn more about the world.

Guests

There are many individuals of an adventurous streak who make a living in the world. When you encounter one of them and yours goals align perhaps they can join your party for a time. Maybe they need help. Maybe you are the ones in need of help. (See the rules for Guests).

Merchant

It is not uncommon for enterprising merchants to travel the lands, especially while making use of roads or when traveling to settlements. In such encounters perhaps such merchants can offer the party some rare items or consumables?

Treasure

Heroes may uncover treasure by chance while traveling through an abandoned area. Such treasure can be a rare ingredient or material, a piece of equipment or perhaps a plot-relevant item that leads to heroes gathering more information.

Vista

During travel one of the possible discoveries is that of a vista. A breathtaking locale or solemn monument. In short, they are memorable places of your party's journey.

When encountering one, the players are incentivized to take the lead in describing it and how it fits with the setting.

If one of the players decides to contribute art for it, they get bonus points! You will want to save it in your album.

When the heroes are in settlement or exploring a location they may want to do certain actions whose resolution should be simple and painless.

These will be covered in this section.

Gathering Information

When the players want to spend time gaining information about people, places or things they can make a @CHECK[ins wlp].

Various skills, equipment and status effects can provide bonuses or inflict maluses on characters. Each bonus belongs to one of the following categories and cannot stack with other bonuses of the same category. Only the highest bonus should be counted.

  • Status: These are temporary and often come from status effects.

  • Skill: These passive bonuses come from character and adversary skills.

  • Equipment: These are provided from equipment such as weapons, armor, etc.

  • Situational: These are based on the character’s tactical positioning.

If you are reading this, I would like to thank you for trying out my foray into designing a virtual tabletop roleplaying game (VTTRPG) that I would like to play at my table with my friends. 

I have been playing RPGs in the digital medium in one form or another for over 30 years. Since 2021 I started dabbling into the TTRPG space and have spent many hours playing them, developing tools for them and thinking about them.

This system is both a passion project and a digital product I wish to keep developing for and make a living from.

If you enjoy your time spent with it, please consider supporting me!

Regards,

Christian Sagel

The design of this system takes inspiration in amounts big and small from the following tabletop role playing systems:

  • Fabula Ultima

  • Pathfinder Second Edition

  • Draw Steel

  • Blades in the Dark

  • Dungeons and Dragons 4th Edition

  • Beacon

It also takes inspiration from various video games I have played over the years:

  • Slay the Spire

  • Final Fantasy Series

  • Tales Of Series

  • World of Warcraft

  • Pillars of Eternity

  • Unicorn Overlord

  • Darkest Dungeon

  • Radiant Historia

This game system has been implemented with the following principles in mind:

  • Every system and rule must justify its place in ink. 

  • Complexity must be minimized wherever possible.

  • Design language should use resonance as much as possible. While some key words may need to be flavored after the system aesthetic, make that the exception rather than the norm.

  • No design survives first contact. The system must be able to evolve and be improved upon user and internal feedback after release.

  • The rules should be intuitive when possible and clearly explained when they cannot.

  • Not everything needs to be made a mechanic out of. Only the things the system cares about should be.

  • Defeat of the player characters is not the end of a campaign, but an opportunity for interesting consequences and a shift in the narrative.

  • Combat is treated as entertainment and not as a sport or war. While it certainly favors the players side, defeat can happen and should be handled gracefully.

  • Balance is a nice goal to have but not at the cost of homogeneity.

  • No character option should eclipse all others in its space so that players would feel compelled to take it every time without question.

  • The system should provide flavoring only as much as is needed to inspire GMs to come up with their own settings.

  • Avoid the use of currency in discrete terms and instead think of it in terms of abstract wealth for the party.

  • No crafting rules.

In the system traits are tags with mechanical connotations associated with them. They can be found in characters and many features such as classes, skills, etc.

Characters gain their traits through class selections whereas adversaries are assigned a number of them depending on their rank.

They are meant to provide an additional layer of texture to differentiate characters from one another, inform their fictional standing and help both players and the director to guide their actions and motivations.

More information on them will be provided in the character creation chapter.

An episode consists of many scenes that stitch the narrative together and propel it forward.

  • Rest: A scene where the party rests for the day.

  • Combat: A scene where the party encounters adversaries in deadly combat.

  • Villain: A scene where the campaign’s adversaries act off-screen.

An individual character's wealth is not tracked by the system. Instead when they enter a settlement and purchase basic goods and services (such as resting in an inn) they are considered to be able to afford them.

Adversaries of elite rank and above can be pressured and eventually staggered.

When an adversary is staggered, they take an increased amount of damage from all sources and  are considered stunned.
